questions.question: Why does the lesson say a decision log that only records 'we picked GPT-4o because it was the best model' fails at the first contract renewal?
options: It doesn't record boundary conditions — the cost threshold, latency SLA, or data classification that would trigger reverting the decision
It doesn't name the model version pinned at selection time
It fails to mention which vendor hosts the model
It was never reviewed by a security architect
questions.explanation: The lesson calls boundary conditions the 'living part' of an AI ADR. Without them recorded, there's nothing to check the decision against when conditions change — the document becomes a museum exhibit rather than something a renewal negotiation can actually use.

questions.question: Which two fields does an AI ADR add on top of the traditional five-field ADR format, according to the lesson's table?
options: Budget and headcount
Trigger conditions and owner/review date
Test coverage and code review sign-off
Marketing approval and legal disclaimer
questions.explanation: Beyond extending status, context, decision, consequences, and alternatives with AI-specific detail, the AI ADR adds trigger conditions (events that mandate re-evaluation) and an owner plus hard review date — neither exists in a traditional ADR, and AI models move faster than annual review cycles.

questions.question: According to the vendor security boundaries section, what distinguishes dedicated provisioned throughput from shared multi-tenant inference?
options: Dedicated throughput is always cheaper per token
Dedicated throughput isolates data from other tenants and gives predictable latency, at higher cost than the shared default
Shared multi-tenant inference is only available for on-premises deployments
Dedicated throughput requires a pinned model version, while shared endpoints never do
questions.explanation: The three endpoint tiers trade cost against isolation: shared multi-tenant is cheapest and default, dedicated provisioned throughput keeps data from mixing across tenants with predictable latency, and on-premises/BYOC gives the strongest isolation at the highest ops cost.

questions.question: The lesson's cost governance formula projects monthly_cost from prompt tokens, completion tokens, daily_requests, and price_per_mtok. What does it warn is the minimum thing this calculation prevents?
options: A model deprecation notice arriving without warning
A 10x traffic spike turning into a budget surprise
A vendor changing its training-data opt-out policy
A latency SLA violation during a regional outage
questions.explanation: The lesson is explicit that this isn't sophisticated modelling — projecting cost at expected production volume rather than prototype volume is the minimum calculation needed so a sudden traffic spike doesn't blow past budget unnoticed.

questions.question: Which of the four standard trigger categories fires when a cheaper-tier model reaches the benchmark score the team originally measured for the more expensive tier?
options: Cost trigger
Capability trigger
Compliance trigger
Deprecation trigger
questions.explanation: The capability trigger specifically covers a new efficient-tier model catching up to the benchmark score recorded at selection time — motivating a downgrade that saves cost without a quality regression, which is exactly why that benchmark needs to be recorded, not just referenced.

questions.question: Why does the lesson say a third-party MCP server should be treated as a vendor relationship in an AI ADR, even though it looks like a library?
options: Because MCP servers always charge per API call
Because it carries its own data classification and vendor accountability for whatever flows through it, the same as any other vendor
Because MCP servers cannot be self-hosted under any circumstances
Because Phase 11 · 14 requires every MCP server to be listed in the register regardless of use
questions.explanation: The lesson connects back to the MCP lesson's framing of tool-call boundaries as scope contracts: an AI ADR should record which MCP server endpoints are used and the data classification of what flows through each, because a third-party server is a real vendor relationship even when it's integrated like a library.
